Accretion (geology).question: What is Accretion (geology)? Geological process by which material is added to a tectonic plate at a subduction zone.
Accretion (geology).fact: In geology, accretion is a process by which material is added to a tectonic plate at a subduction zone, frequently on the edge of existing continental landmasses.   The added material may be sediment, volcanic arcs, seamounts, oceanic crust or other igneous features.

Antarctic.subject: World Geography
Antarctic.question: What is Antarctic? Polar region around Earth's South Pole.
Antarctic.fact: The Antarctic (; US also , commonly ) is the polar region of Earth that surrounds the South Pole, lying within the Antarctic Circle.   The Antarctic comprises the continent of Antarctica, the Kerguelen Plateau, and other island territories located on the Antarctic Plate or south of the Antarctic Convergence.

Antarctic Convergence.subject: World Geography
Antarctic Convergence.question: What is Antarctic Convergence? Separation of two hydrological & climatic regions.
Antarctic Convergence.fact: The Antarctic Convergence or Antarctic Polar Front is a marine belt encircling Antarctica where cold, northward-flowing Antarctic waters meet the warmer waters of the sub-Antarctic.

Antarctic Peninsula.question: What is Antarctic Peninsula? Peninsula located in northern Antarctica.
Antarctic Peninsula.fact: The Antarctic Peninsula, called O'Higgins Land in Chile and Tierra de San Martin in Argentina, and originally as Graham Land in the United Kingdom and the Palmer Peninsula in the United States, is the northernmost part of mainland Antarctica.   The Antarctic Peninsula is part of the larger peninsula of West Antarctica, protruding 1,300 km (810 miles) from a line between Cape Adams (Weddell Sea) and a point on the mainland south of the Eklund Islands.

Antarctic Plateau.question: What is Antarctic Plateau? Plateau of East Antarctica.
Antarctic Plateau.fact: The Antarctic Plateau, Polar Plateau or King Haakon VII Plateau is a large area of East Antarctica that extends over a diameter of about 1,000 kilometres (620 mi), and includes the region of the geographic South Pole and the Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station.

Aggradation.subject: World Geography
Aggradation.question: What is Aggradation? Increase in land elevation due to the deposition of sediment.
Aggradation.fact: Aggradation (or alluviation) in geology is the increase in land elevation, typically in a river system, due to the deposition of sediment.   Aggradation occurs in areas in which the supply of sediment is greater than the amount of material that the system is able to transport.

Angle of attack.subject: World Geography
Angle of attack.question: What is Angle of attack? Angle between the chord of a wing and the undisturbed airflow.
Angle of attack.fact: In fluid dynamics, angle of attack (AOA, α, or α {\displaystyle \alpha } ) is the angle between a reference line on a body (often the chord line of an airfoil) and the vector representing the relative motion between the body and the fluid through which it is moving.   Angle of attack is the angle between the body's reference line and the oncoming flow.

Armor (hydrology).subject: World Geography
Armor (hydrology).question: What is Armor (hydrology)? Association of surface rocks with stream beds or beaches.
Armor (hydrology).fact: In hydrology and geography, armor is the association of surface pebbles, rocks or boulders with stream beds or beaches.   Most commonly hydrological armor occurs naturally; however, a man-made form is usually called riprap, when shorelines or stream banks are fortified for erosion protection with large boulders or sizable manufactured concrete objects.

Backwater (river).subject: World Geography
Backwater (river).question: What is Backwater (river)? River section with little or no current.
Backwater (river).fact: A backwater is a relatively stagnant part of a river in which there is little or no current.   It can refer to a small anabranch of a main river, which diverges from and meanders alongside the main stem before rejoining it downstreams, and thus carrying a significantly weaker flow; or an ectopic stream pool extend from the side of a watercourse backed up by reverse flow from tides (as in the case of tidal rivers) or due to increased flow resistance caused by obstacles such as a weir, dam or l...

Baer–Babinet law.subject: World Geography
Baer–Babinet law.question: What is Baer–Babinet law? Theory on the formation of rivers due to Earth's rotation.
Baer–Babinet law.fact: In geography, the Baer–Babinet law, sometimes called Baer's law, identifies a way in which the process of formation of rivers is influenced by the rotation of the Earth.

Breakwater (structure).subject: World Geography
Breakwater (structure).question: What is Breakwater (structure)? Coastal defense structure.
Breakwater (structure).fact: A breakwater is a permanent structure constructed at a coastal area to protect against tides, currents, waves, and storm surges.   Breakwaters have been built since antiquity to protect anchorages, helping isolate vessels from marine hazards such as wind-driven waves.

Bridge.subject: World Geography
Bridge.question: What is Bridge? Structure built to span physical obstacles.
Bridge.fact: A bridge is a structure designed to span an obstacle, such as a river or railway, allowing vehicles, pedestrians, and other loads to pass across.   Most bridges consist of a flat deck, supported by beams, arches, or cables.

Abutment.subject: World Geography
Abutment.question: What is Abutment? Construction substructure.
Abutment.fact: An abutment is the substructure at the ends of a bridge span or dam supporting its superstructure.   Single-span bridges have abutments at each end that provide vertical and lateral support for the span, as well as acting as retaining walls to resist lateral movement of the earthen fill of the bridge approach.

Custer Creek train wreck.subject: World Geography
Custer Creek train wreck.question: What is Custer Creek train wreck? Train wreck outside of Saugus, Montana.
Custer Creek train wreck.fact: The Custer Creek train wreck (sometimes called the Saugus train wreck) is the worst rail disaster in Montana history.

Engineering.subject: World Geography
Engineering.question: What is Engineering? Applied science and research.
Engineering.fact: Engineering is the practice of systematically applying natural science and mathematics to design and improve systems, devices, or processes that solve problems under constraints.   Engineering involves balancing competing demands such as safety, performance, aesthetics, cost, laws and regulations, and time, while operating within fundamental limits such as the laws of physics.

Check dam.subject: World Geography
Check dam.question: What is Check dam? Small dam to counteract erosion.
Check dam.fact: A check dam is a small, sometimes temporary, dam constructed across a swale, drainage ditch, or waterway to counteract erosion by reducing water flow velocity.   Check dams themselves are not a type of new technology; rather, they are an ancient technique dating from the second century AD.

Federal Highway Administration.subject: World Geography
Federal Highway Administration.question: What is Federal Highway Administration? US highway transportation agency.
Federal Highway Administration.fact: The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) is a division of the United States Department of Transportation that specializes in highway transportation.

Federal Highway Administration.fact: In 1910, the American Association for Highway Improvement was organized.

Fluid dynamics.subject: World Geography
Fluid dynamics.question: What is Fluid dynamics? Aspects of fluid mechanics involving fluid flow.
Fluid dynamics.fact: In physics, physical chemistry, and engineering, fluid dynamics is a subdiscipline of fluid mechanics that describes the flow of fluids – liquids and gases.   Fluid dynamics has a wide range of applications, including calculating forces and moments on aircraft, determining the mass flow rate of petroleum through pipelines, predicting weather patterns, understanding nebulae in interstellar space, understanding large scale geophysical flows involving oceans/atmosphere and modelling fission weap...

Flume.subject: World Geography
Flume.question: What is Flume? Human-made channel for water.
Flume.fact: A flume is a human-made channel for water, in the form of an open declined gravity chute whose walls are raised above the surrounding terrain, in contrast to a trench or ditch.   Flumes are not to be confused with aqueducts, which are built to transport water; flumes use flowing water to transport materials.

Gabion.subject: World Geography
Gabion.question: What is Gabion? Cage full of rock.
Gabion.fact: A gabion (from Italian gabbione meaning "big cage"; from Italian gabbia and Latin cavea meaning "cage") is a cage, cylinder, or cube, typically mesh, filled with solid material suitable to use in various civil engineering and military applications.   Among the most common civil engineering uses are erosion control, retaining walls, and impact attenuation; in the military gabions commonly protect forward operating bases and artillery firing positions against small arms and indirect fragmentary...

Gabion.question: The Maccaferri family produced sack-shaped gabions starting in _____
Gabion.fact: The Maccaferri family produced sack-shaped gabions starting in 1893.

Glanrhyd Bridge collapse.fact: On 19 October 1987, a train on the Heart of Wales line derailed and fell into the River Towy due to the partial collapse of the Glanrhyd Bridge near Llandeilo, Carmarthenshire. Gravel.subject: World Geography
Gravel.question: What is Gravel? Mix of crumbled stones.
Gravel.fact: Gravel () is a loose aggregation of rock fragments.   Gravel occurs naturally on Earth as a result of sedimentary and erosive geological processes; it is also produced in large quantities commercially as crushed stone.

Grout.subject: World Geography
Grout.question: What is Grout? Building material.
Grout.fact: Grout is a dense substance that flows like a liquid yet hardens upon application, often used to fill gaps or to function as reinforcement in existing structures.   Grout is generally a mixture of water, cement, and sand, and is frequently employed in efforts such as pressure grouting, embedding rebar in masonry walls, connecting sections of precast concrete, filling voids, and sealing joints such as those between tiles.

Groyne.subject: World Geography
Groyne.question: What is Groyne? Structure extending into a body of water to alter water flow.
Groyne.fact: A groyne (British English) or groin (American English; see spelling differences) is a rigid aquatic structure built perpendicularly from an ocean shore (in coastal engineering) or a river bank, interrupting water flow and limiting the movement of sediment.   In the ocean, groynes create beaches, prevent beach erosion caused by longshore drift where this is the dominant process and facilitate beach nourishment.

Highway.subject: World Geography
Highway.question: What is Highway? Public road or other public way on land.
Highway.fact: A highway in the broadest sense of the term is any public or private road or other public way on land, including not just major roads but also other public roads and rights of way.   It is sometimes used casually as a synonym of freeway, or expressway, denoting a controlled-access highway.

Abiotic component.subject: World Geography
Abiotic component.question: What is Abiotic component? Non-living factors that affect organisms and ecosystems.
Abiotic component.fact: In ecology, abiotic components or abiotic factors are non-living chemical and physical parts of the environment that affect living organisms and the functioning of ecosystems.

Abiotic stress.subject: World Geography
Abiotic stress.question: What is Abiotic stress? Stress on organisms caused by nonliving factors.
Abiotic stress.fact: Abiotic stress is the negative impact of non-living factors on the living organisms in a specific environment.   Whereas a biotic stress would include living disturbances such as fungi or harmful insects, abiotic stress factors, or stressors, are naturally occurring, often intangible and inanimate factors such as intense sunlight, temperature or wind that may cause harm to the plants and animals in the area affected.

Abundance (ecology).subject: World Geography
Abundance (ecology).question: What is Abundance (ecology)? Relative representation of a species in an ecosystem.
Abundance (ecology).fact: In ecology, local abundance is the relative representation of a species in a particular ecosystem.   It is usually measured as the number of individuals found per sample.

Adaptive radiation.subject: World Geography
Adaptive radiation.question: What is Adaptive radiation? Process in which organisms diversify rapidly from an ancestral species.
Adaptive radiation.fact: In evolutionary biology, adaptive radiation is a process in which organisms diversify rapidly from an ancestral species into a multitude of new forms, particularly when a change in the environment makes new resources available, alters biotic interactions or opens new environmental niches.   The prototypical example of adaptive radiation is finch speciation on the Galapagos ("Darwin's finches"), but examples are known from around the world.

Adenosine triphosphate.subject: World Geography
Adenosine triphosphate.question: What is Adenosine triphosphate? Energy-carrying molecule in living cells.

Aerobiology.subject: World Geography
Aerobiology.question: What is Aerobiology? Study of airborne organisms.
Aerobiology.fact: Aerobiology (from Greek ἀήρ, aēr, "air"; βίος, bios, "life"; and -λογία, -logia) is a branch of biology that studies the passive transport of organic particles, such as bacteria, fungal spores, very small insects, pollen grains and viruses.   However, aerobiology is a varied field, relating to environmental science, plant science, meteorology, phenology, and climate change.

Afrotropical realm.subject: World Geography
Afrotropical realm.question: What is Afrotropical realm? One of Earth's eight biogeographic realms.
Afrotropical realm.fact: The Afrotropical realm is one of the Earth's eight biogeographic realms.

Agronomy.subject: World Geography
Agronomy.question: What is Agronomy? Science of producing and using plants.
Agronomy.fact: Agronomy is the sub-discipline of plant agriculture focused on the science and technology of crop production and soil management as it pertains to field crops in the context of industrial agriculture and cultivation with Intensive farming methods.   Agronomy has come to include the research of plant genetics, plant physiology, meteorology, and soil science.

Abiogenesis.subject: World Geography
Abiogenesis.question: What is Abiogenesis? Life arising from non-living matter.
Abiogenesis.fact: Abiogenesis or the origin of life (sometimes called biopoiesis) is the natural process by which life arises from non-living matter, such as simple organic compounds.   The study of abiogenesis aims to determine how pre-life chemical reactions gave rise to life under conditions strikingly different from those on Earth today.

Alexander von Humboldt.question: What is Alexander von Humboldt? German polymath (1769–1859).
Alexander von Humboldt.fact: Friedrich Wilhelm Heinrich Alexander von Humboldt (14 September 1769 – 6 May 1859) was a German polymath, geographer, naturalist, explorer, and proponent of Romantic philosophy and science.

Alfred Russel Wallace.subject: World Geography
Alfred Russel Wallace.question: What is Alfred Russel Wallace? English naturalist (1823–1913).
Alfred Russel Wallace.fact: Alfred Russel Wallace (8 January 1823 – 7 November 1913) was an English naturalist, explorer, geographer, anthropologist, biologist and illustrator.

Alfred Russel Wallace.question: He independently conceived the theory of evolution through natural selection; his _____ paper on the subject was published that year alongside extracts from Charles Darwin's writings on the topic
Alfred Russel Wallace.fact: He independently conceived the theory of evolution through natural selection; his 1858 paper on the subject was published that year alongside extracts from Charles Darwin's writings on the topic.

Alfred Russel Wallace.question: It spurred Darwin to set aside the "big species book" he was drafting and to quickly write an abstract of it, which was published in _____ as On the Origin of Species

Alfred Russel Wallace.question: Wallace's _____ book Man's Place in the Universe was the first serious attempt by a biologist to evaluate the likelihood of life on other planets
Alfred Russel Wallace.fact: Wallace's 1904 book Man's Place in the Universe was the first serious attempt by a biologist to evaluate the likelihood of life on other planets.

Agrostology.subject: World Geography
Agrostology.question: What is Agrostology? Scientific study of the grasses.
Agrostology.fact: Agrostology (from Greek ἄγρωστις, agrōstis, "type of grass"; and -λογία, -logia), sometimes graminology, is the scientific study of the grasses (the family Poaceae, or Gramineae).   The grasslike species of the sedge family (Cyperaceae), the rush family (Juncaceae), and the bulrush or cattail family (Typhaceae) are often included with the true grasses in the category of graminoid, although strictly speaking these are not included within the study of agrostology.

Allee effect.subject: World Geography
Allee effect.question: What is Allee effect? Population phenomenon in biology.
Allee effect.fact: The Allee effect is a phenomenon in biology characterized by a correlation between population size or density and the mean individual fitness (often measured as per capita population growth rate) of a population or species.

Allen's rule.subject: World Geography
Allen's rule.question: What is Allen's rule? Relation of habitat temperature and limb length.
Allen's rule.fact: Allen's rule is an ecogeographical rule formulated by Joel Asaph Allen in 1877, broadly stating that animals adapted to cold climates have shorter and thicker limbs and bodily appendages than animals adapted to warm climates.   Because animals living in cold climates need to conserve as much heat as possible, Allen's rule predicts that they should have evolved comparatively low surface area-to-volume ratios to minimize the surface area by which they dissipate heat, allowing them to retain mor...

Allen's rule.fact: Allen's rule is an ecogeographical rule formulated by Joel Asaph Allen in 1877, broadly stating that animals adapted to cold climates have shorter and thicker limbs and bodily appendages than animals adapted to warm climates.

Allometry.subject: World Geography
Allometry.question: What is Allometry? Study of the relationship of body size to shape, anatomy, physiology, and behavior.
Allometry.fact: Allometry (Ancient Greek ἄλλος állos "other", μέτρον métron "measurement") is the study of the relationship of body size to shape, anatomy, physiology and behaviour, first outlined by Otto Snell in 1892, by D'Arcy Thompson in 1917 in On Growth and Form and by Julian Huxley in 1932.

Allopatric speciation.subject: World Geography
Allopatric speciation.question: What is Allopatric speciation? Speciation that occurs between geographically isolated populations.
Allopatric speciation.fact: Allopatric speciation is a mode of speciation that occurs when biological populations become geographically isolated from each other to an extent that prevents or interferes with gene flow.

Alternative stable state.subject: World Geography
Alternative stable state.question: What is Alternative stable state? Ecological concept.
Alternative stable state.fact: In ecology, the theory of alternative stable states (sometimes termed alternate stable states or alternative stable equilibria) predicts that ecosystems can exist under multiple "states" (sets of unique biotic and abiotic conditions).

Altitudinal zonation.subject: World Geography
Altitudinal zonation.question: What is Altitudinal zonation? Natural layering of ecosystems by elevation.
Altitudinal zonation.fact: Altitudinal zonation (or elevational zonation) in mountainous regions describes the natural layering of ecosystems that occurs at distinct elevations due to varying environmental conditions.   Altitudinal zonation was first hypothesized by geographer Alexander von Humboldt who noticed that temperature drops with increasing elevation.

Amino acid.subject: World Geography
Amino acid.question: What is Amino acid? Organic compounds containing amine and carboxylic groups.
Amino acid.fact: Amino acids are organic compounds that contain both amino and carboxylic acid functional groups.   Although over 500 amino acids exist in nature, by far the most important are the 22 α-amino acids incorporated into proteins.

Animal migration.subject: World Geography
Animal migration.question: What is Animal migration? Periodic large-scale movement of animals, usually seasonal.
Animal migration.fact: Animal migration is the relatively long-distance movement of individual animals, usually on a seasonal basis.

Anchialine system.subject: World Geography
Anchialine system.question: What is Anchialine system? Landlocked body of water with underground connection to the sea.
Anchialine system.fact: An anchialine system (, from Greek ankhialos 'near the sea') is a landlocked body of water with a subterranean connection to the ocean.

Atmospheric science.subject: World Geography
Atmospheric science.question: What is Atmospheric science? Study of the atmosphere, its processes, and its interactions with other systems.
Atmospheric science.fact: Atmospheric science is the study of the Earth's atmosphere and its various inner-working physical processes.

Avulsion (river).subject: World Geography
Avulsion (river).question: What is Avulsion (river)? Rapid abandonment of a river channel and formation of a new channel.
Avulsion (river).fact: In sedimentary geology and fluvial geomorphology, avulsion is the process by which flow is diverted out of an set up river channel and into a new course via a bifurcation, or splitting of the channel.   Avulsions range from full, in which all flow is diverted from one channel to another, to partial, in which only a portion of flow is diverted.

Ayre (landform).subject: World Geography
Ayre (landform).question: What is Ayre (landform)? Shingle beaches in Orkney and Shetland.
Ayre (landform).fact: An ayre (Shaetlan pronunciation: [eər] AIR) is the name used for shingle beaches found in Orkney, Shetland, the Isle of Man, Lancashire, Cumbria and Northumbria.   The word is derived from the Old Norse eyrr, meaning a shingle beach or gravelly place, and may be applied to ordinary beaches, cliff-foot beaches such as the Lang Ayre in Northmavine, Shetland, spits, bars or tombolos, but only if formed of shingle.

Accretion (coastal management).subject: World Geography
Accretion (coastal management).question: What is Accretion (coastal management)? Process of coastal sediment returning to the visible portion of a beach.
Accretion (coastal management).fact: Accretion is the process of coastal sediment returning to the visible portion of a beach or foreshore after a submersion event.   A sustainable beach or foreshore often goes through a cycle of submersion during rough weather and later accretion during calmer periods.

Bay.subject: World Geography
Bay.question: What is Bay? Recessed, coastal body of water connected to an ocean or lake.
Bay.fact: A bay is a recessed, coastal body of water that directly connects to a larger main body of water, such as an ocean, a lake, or another bay.   A large bay is usually called a gulf, sea, sound, or bight.

Beach.subject: World Geography
Beach.question: What is Beach? Area of loose particles at the edge of a body of water.
Beach.fact: A beach is a landform alongside a body of water which consists of loose particles.   The particles composing a beach are typically made from rock, such as sand, gravel, shingle, pebbles, etc.

Beach cusps.subject: World Geography
Beach cusps.question: What is Beach cusps? Shoreline formations made up of various grades of sediment in an arc pattern.
Beach cusps.fact: Beach cusps are shoreline formations made up of various grades of sediment in an arc pattern.

Barrier island.subject: World Geography
Barrier island.question: What is Barrier island? Coastal dune landform that forms by wave and tidal action parallel to the mainland coast.
Barrier island.fact: Barrier islands are a coastal landform, a type of dune system and sand island, where an area of sand off the coast has been formed by wave and tidal action parallel to the mainland coast.   Barrier islands are commonly formed in long, narrow systems parallel to shorelines and are shaped by waves, tides, sediment movement, and sea-level change, which cause them to shift, grow, or erode over time.

Beach evolution.subject: World Geography
Beach evolution.question: What is Beach evolution? Changes to a shoreline by accretion and erosion.
Beach evolution.fact: Beach evolution is a natural process occurring along shorelines where sea, lake, or river water erodes the land.   Catastrophic events such as tsunamis, hurricanes, and storm surges accelerate beach evolution.

Beach nourishment.subject: World Geography
Beach nourishment.question: What is Beach nourishment? Sediment replacement process.
Beach nourishment.fact: Beach nourishment (also called beach renourishment, beach replenishment, or sand replenishment) describes a process by which sediment, usually sand, lost through longshore drift or erosion is replaced from other sources.   Beach nourishment is typically part of a larger integrated coastal zone management aimed at coastal defense.

Beach ridge.fact: A beach ridge is a wave-swept or wave-deposited ridge running parallel to a shoreline.

Beach wrack.fact: Beach wrack or marine wrack is organic material (e.

100-year flood.subject: World Geography
100-year flood.question: What is 100-year flood? Indication of the likelihood of a flooding.
100-year flood.fact: A 100-year flood, also called a 1% flood, or High Probability in the UK, is a flood event for a defined location at a level reached or exceeded once per hundred years, on average, but as there are many locations there are multiple independent 100-year floods within the same year.

Aber and Inver (placename elements).subject: World Geography
Aber and Inver (placename elements).question: What is Aber and Inver (placename elements)? Common elements in place-names of Celtic origin.
Aber and Inver (placename elements).fact: Aber and Inver are common elements in place-names of Celtic origin.   Both mean "confluence of waters" or "river mouth".

Abrasion (geology).subject: World Geography
Abrasion (geology).question: What is Abrasion (geology)? Process of erosion.
Abrasion (geology).fact: Abrasion is a process of weathering that occurs when material being transported wears away at a surface over time, commonly occurring with ice and glaciers.   The primary process of abrasion is physical weathering.

Acid mine drainage.subject: World Geography
Acid mine drainage.question: What is Acid mine drainage? Outflow of acidic water from metal or coal mines.
Acid mine drainage.fact: Acid mine drainage, acid and metalliferous drainage (AMD), or acid rock drainage (ARD) is the outflow of acidic water from metal mines and coal mines.

Ait.subject: World Geography
Ait.question: What is Ait? Small river islands (British English).
Ait.fact: An ait (, like eight) or eyot () is a small island.   Aits are typically formed by the deposit of sediment in the water, which accumulates.

Al-Qurnah.fact: Al-Qurnah (Kurnah or Qurna, meaning connection/joint in Arabic) is a town in southern Iraq about 74 km northwest of Basra, that lies within the conglomeration of Nahairat.

Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, Nizhny Novgo.subject: World Geography
Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, Nizhny Novgo.question: What is Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, Nizhny Novgorod? Church in Nizhny Novgorod, Russia.
Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, Nizhny Novgo.fact: The Alexander Nevsky Cathedral (Russian: Собор Святого Александра Невского) is a Russian Orthodox cathedral church in the Kanavinsky city district of Nizhny Novgorod.   The cathedral is located on the former territory of the Nizhny Novgorod Fair.

Allegheny River.subject: World Geography
Allegheny River.question: What is Allegheny River? River in Northeastern United States.
Allegheny River.fact: The Allegheny River ( AL-ig-AY-nee; Seneca: Ohi:yo'; Unami: Alikehane) is a 325-mile-long (523 km) river that is in western Pennsylvania and western New York in the United States.   The Allegheny River is, by volume, the main headstream of both the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers.

Allegheny River.subject: World Geography
Allegheny River.question: A 24-mile-long portion of the upper river in Warren and McKean counties of Pennsylvania and Cattaraugus County in New York forms the Allegheny Reservoir, which was created by the erection of the Kinzu
Allegheny River.fact: A 24-mile-long portion of the upper river in Warren and McKean counties of Pennsylvania and Cattaraugus County in New York forms the Allegheny Reservoir, which was created by the erection of the Kinzua Dam in 1965 for flood control.

Alluvial river.subject: World Geography
Alluvial river.question: What is Alluvial river? Type of river.
Alluvial river.fact: An alluvial river is one in which the bed and stream banks are made up of mobile sediment or soil.   Alluvial rivers are self-formed, meaning that their channels are shaped by the magnitude and frequency of the floods that they experience, and the ability of these floods to erode, deposit, and transport sediment.

Anabranch.subject: World Geography
Anabranch.question: What is Anabranch? Part of a river or stream that diverts from and rejoins the main channel.
Anabranch.fact: An anabranch is a section of a river or stream that diverts from the main channel or stem of the watercourse and rejoins the main stem downstream.   Local anabranches can be the result of small islands in the watercourse.

Angela Gurnell.subject: World Geography
Angela Gurnell.question: What is Angela Gurnell? British geoscientist.
Angela Gurnell.fact: Angela Gurnell is a British geoscientist who is Professor of Physical Geography at Queen Mary University of London.

Angela Gurnell.fact: In 2010 Gurnell left King's College to join Queen Mary University of London.

Aquatic toxicology.subject: World Geography
Aquatic toxicology.question: What is Aquatic toxicology? Study of manufactured products on aquatic organisms.
Aquatic toxicology.fact: Aquatic toxicology is the study of the effects of manufactured chemicals and other anthropogenic and natural materials and activities on aquatic organisms at various levels of organization, from subcellular through individual organisms to communities and ecosystems.   Aquatic toxicology is a multidisciplinary field which integrates toxicology, aquatic ecology and aquatic chemistry.

Antecedent drainage stream.subject: World Geography
Antecedent drainage stream.question: What is Antecedent drainage stream? Stream maintaining its original course despite changes in underlying rocks.
Antecedent drainage stream.fact: An antecedent stream is a stream that maintains its original course and pattern despite the changes in underlying rock topography.   A stream with a dendritic drainage pattern, for example, can be subject to slow tectonic uplift.

Aragvi.subject: World Geography
Aragvi.question: What is Aragvi? River in Georgia.
Aragvi.fact: The Aragvi (Georgian: არაგვი, romanized: aragvi [ˈäɾägvi]) and its basin are in Georgia on the southern slopes of the Caucasus Mountains.

Acid sulfate soil.subject: World Geography
Acid sulfate soil.question: What is Acid sulfate soil? Soils formed under waterlogged conditions.
Acid sulfate soil.fact: Acid sulfate soils are naturally occurring soils, sediments or organic substrates (e.   In an undisturbed state below the water table, acid sulfate soils are benign.

Contour line.subject: World Geography
Contour line.question: What is Contour line? Curve along which a 3-D surface is at equal elevation.
Contour line.fact: A contour line (also isoline, isopleth, isoquant or isarithm) of a function of two variables is a curve along which the function has a constant value, so that the curve joins points of equal value to the state.   More generally, a contour line for a function of two variables is a curve connecting points where the function has the same particular value.

Crop.subject: World Geography
Crop.question: What is Crop? Plant product which can be grown and harvested.
Crop.fact: A crop is a plant or plant product harvested for human use.   Crops are cultivated at scale to produce food, fiber, fuel, and other products.

Ditch.subject: World Geography
Ditch.question: What is Ditch? Small to moderate trench created to channel water.
Ditch.fact: A ditch is a small-to-moderate size trench created to channel water.   A ditch can be used for drainage, to drain water from low-lying areas, alongside roadways or fields, or to channel water from a more distant source for plant irrigation.

Drainage.subject: World Geography
Drainage.question: What is Drainage? Removal of water from an area of land.
Drainage.fact: Drainage is the natural or artificial removal of a surface's water and sub-surface water from an area with excess water.   The internal drainage of most agricultural soils can prevent severe waterlogging (anaerobic conditions that harm root growth), but many soils need artificial drainage to improve production or to manage water supplies.

Drainage equation.subject: World Geography
Drainage equation.question: What is Drainage equation? Equation used in drainage design.
Drainage equation.fact: A drainage equation is an equation describing the relation between depth and spacing of parallel subsurface drains, depth of the watertable, depth and hydraulic conductivity of the soils.   A well known steady-state drainage equation is the Hooghoudt drain spacing equation.

Drainage research.subject: World Geography
Drainage research.question: What is Drainage research? Study of agricultural drainage systems.
Drainage research.fact: Drainage research is the study of agricultural drainage systems and their effects to arrive at optimal system design.   All these aspects can be subject of drainage research.

Environmental impact of irrigation.subject: World Geography
Environmental impact of irrigation.question: What is Land & irrigation?
Environmental impact of irrigation.fact: The environmental impact of irrigation relates to the changes in quantity and quality of soil and water as a result of irrigation and the subsequent effects on natural and social conditions in river basins and downstream of an irrigation scheme.

Grass.subject: World Geography
Grass.question: What is Grass? Collective name for three families of plants.
Grass.fact: Grass refers to various families of plants.   The three major families of grasslike plants are true grasses (Poaceae), sedges (Cyperaceae), and rushes (Juncaceae).

Groundwater flow.subject: World Geography
Groundwater flow.question: What is Groundwater flow? Groundwater discharge into a stream.
Groundwater flow.fact: In hydrogeology, groundwater flow is defined as the "part of streamflow that has infiltrated the ground, entered the phreatic zone, and has been (or is at a particular time) discharged into a stream channel or springs; and seepage water.  " It is governed by the groundwater flow equation.

Groundwater model.subject: World Geography
Groundwater model.question: What is Groundwater model? Computer models of groundwater flow systems.
Groundwater model.fact: Groundwater models are computer models of groundwater flow systems, and are used by hydrologists and hydrogeologists.   Groundwater models are used to simulate and predict aquifer conditions.

Groundwater recharge.subject: World Geography
Groundwater recharge.question: What is Groundwater recharge? Groundwater that recharges an aquifer.
Groundwater recharge.fact: Groundwater recharge or deep drainage or deep percolation is a hydrologic process, where water moves downward from surface water to groundwater.   Groundwater recharge also encompasses water moving away from the water table farther into the saturated zone.

Drip irrigation.subject: World Geography
Drip irrigation.question: What is Drip irrigation? Irrigation system.
Drip irrigation.fact: Drip irrigation or trickle irrigation is a type of micro-irrigation system that has the potential to save water and nutrients by allowing water to drip slowly to the roots of plants, either from above the soil surface or buried below the surface.   Drip irrigation systems distribute water through a network of valves, pipes, tubing, and emitters.

Drip irrigation.subject: World Geography
Drip irrigation.question: As of _____, 3% of the world's farmers use drip irrigation
Drip irrigation.fact: As of 2023, 3% of the world's farmers use drip irrigation.

Drip irrigation.fact: The first experimental system of this type was set up in 1959 by Blass, who partnered later in 1964 with Kibbutz Hatzerim to create an irrigation company called Netafim.

Hydraulic conductivity.subject: World Geography
Hydraulic conductivity.question: What is Hydraulic conductivity? Ability of water to flow through a porous material.
Hydraulic conductivity.fact: In science and engineering, hydraulic conductivity (K, in SI units of meters per second) is a property of porous materials, soils and rocks, that describes the ease with which a fluid (usually water) can move through the pore space, or fracture network.   Saturated hydraulic conductivity, Ksat, describes water movement through saturated media.

Hydrological model.subject: World Geography
Hydrological model.question: What is Hydrological model? Predicting and managing water resources.
Hydrological model.fact: A hydrologic model is a simplification of a real-world system (e.  , surface water, soil water, wetland, groundwater, estuary) that aids in understanding, predicting, and managing water resources.

Hydrological transport model.subject: World Geography
Hydrological transport model.question: What is Hydrological transport model? Type of mathematical model.
Hydrological transport model.fact: An hydrological transport model is a mathematical model used to simulate the flow of rivers, streams, groundwater movement or drainage front displacement, and calculate water quality parameters.

Growing season.subject: World Geography
Growing season.question: What is Growing season? Portion of the year in which local conditions permit normal plant growth.
Growing season.fact: The growing season is that portion of the year in which local conditions (i.   While each plant or crop has a specific growing season that depends on its genetic adaptation, growing seasons can generally be grouped into macro-environmental classes.

Aiguille Verte.subject: World Geography
Aiguille Verte.question: What is Aiguille Verte? Mountain in the Mont Blanc massif in the French Alps.
Aiguille Verte.fact: The Aiguille Verte (French pronunciation: [eɡɥij vɛʁt]; 4,122 m (13,524 ft)), is a mountain in the Mont Blanc massif in the French Alps.   Aiguille Verte is French for "Green Needle", which is the meaning commonly attributed to the name.

Aiguille du Dru.subject: World Geography
Aiguille du Dru.question: What is Aiguille du Dru? Mountain in the Mont Blanc massif in the French Alps.
Aiguille du Dru.fact: The Aiguille du Dru (also the Dru or the Drus; French, Les Drus) is a mountain in the Mont Blanc massif in the French Alps.   The mountain's highest summit is: Grande Aiguille du Dru (or the Grand Dru) 3,754 m Another, slightly lower sub-summit is: Petite Aiguille du Dru (or the Petit Dru) 3,733 m.

Ammergau Alps.question: What is Ammergau Alps? Mountain range in the states of Bavaria, Germany and Tyrol, Austria.
Ammergau Alps.fact: The Ammergau Alps (German: Ammergauer Alpen or Ammergebirge) are a mountain range in the Northern Limestone Alps in the states of Bavaria (Germany) and Tyrol (Austria).

Ancohuma.subject: World Geography
Ancohuma.question: What is Ancohuma? Mountain in Bolivia.
Ancohuma.fact: Ancohuma or Janq'u Uma (Aymara janq'u white, uma water, "white water", also spelled Janq'uma, other spellings, Jankho Uma, Jankhouma) is the third highest mountain in Bolivia (after Sajama and Illimani).   Despite being higher than Illampu, Ancohuma is a gentler peak, with less local relief, and it is a somewhat easier climb.

Banff National Park.question: What is Banff National Park? National park in Alberta, Canada.
Banff National Park.fact: Banff National Park is Canada's first national park, set up in 1885 as Rocky Mountains Park.

Banff National Park.question: Banff National Park is Canada's first national park, established in _____ as Rocky Mountains Park
Banff National Park.fact: Banff National Park is Canada's first national park, set up in 1885 as Rocky Mountains Park.

Berguedà.subject: World Geography
Berguedà.question: What is Berguedà? Comarca in Catalonia, Spain.
Berguedà.fact: Berguedà (Catalan pronunciation: [bəɾɣəˈða]) is an inland comarca in the central region of Catalonia, Spain.   Its northern border is a veritable mountain barrier: Berguedà is separated from Cerdanya by a chain of 2,000-meter peaks.

Bohemia.subject: World Geography
Bohemia.question: What is Bohemia? Historical region in the Czech Republic.
Bohemia.fact: Bohemia ( boh-HEE-mee-ə; Czech: Čechy [ˈtʃɛxɪ] ; German: Böhmen [ˈbøːmən] ) is the westernmost and largest historical region of the Czech Republic.   Bohemia can also refer to a wider area consisting of the historical Lands of the Bohemian Crown ruled by the Bohemian kings, including Moravia and Czech Silesia, in which case the term refers to the historical cultural and political space of the Czech people.

Bohemia.question: Between _____ and 1945, these border regions were annexed to Nazi Germany as the Sudetenland
Bohemia.fact: Between 1938 and 1945, these border regions were annexed to Nazi Germany as the Sudetenland.

Bohemia.question: In _____, the Czech lands (including Bohemia) were invaded by Warsaw Pact troops sent by the Soviet Union and stayed under occupation as the Czech Socialist Republic until the Velvet Revolution in 198
Bohemia.fact: In 1968, the Czech lands (including Bohemia) were invaded by Warsaw Pact troops sent by the Soviet Union and stayed under occupation as the Czech Socialist Republic until the Velvet Revolution in 1989.

Bohemia.question: In _____, the name was changed to the Czech Republic, which became a separate state in 1993 with the breakup of Czechoslovakia
Bohemia.fact: In 1990, the name was changed to the Czech Republic, which became a separate state in 1993 with the breakup of Czechoslovakia.

Bolivia.subject: World Geography
Bolivia.question: What is Bolivia? Country in South America.
Bolivia.fact: Bolivia, officially the Plurinational State of Bolivia, is a landlocked country in central South America.

Brecon Beacons.subject: World Geography
Brecon Beacons.question: What is Brecon Beacons? Mountain range in Wales.
Brecon Beacons.fact: The Brecon Beacons (Welsh: Bannau Brycheiniog; [ˈbanai̯ brəˈχei̯njɔɡ] ) are a mountain range in Wales.   The Brecon Beacons have given their name to the larger Brecon Beacons National Park, and the range itself is therefore sometimes called the Central Beacons to differentiate the two.

Broad Peak.subject: World Geography
Broad Peak.question: What is 12th-highest mountain on Earth?
Broad Peak.fact: Broad Peak is one of the eight-thousanders, and is in the Karakoram range spanning Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan and Xinjiang, China.

Chogolisa.subject: World Geography
Chogolisa.question: What is Chogolisa? Mountain in Pakistan.
Chogolisa.fact: Chogolisa (Urdu: چوگولیزا derived from Chogo Ling Sa; literally "Great Hunt") is a trapezoidal mountain in the Karakoram range within the Gilgit-Baltistan region of Pakistan.   Chogolisa has several peaks, the highest being its southwest face (Chogolisa I), which reaches an elevation of 7,665 metres (25,148 ft).

Chogolisa.fact: On the northeast side, the second-highest peak stands at 7,654 m (25,112 ft) in height and was named "Bride Peak" by Martin Conway in 1892.

Chogolisa.fact: Austrian mountaineers Hermann Buhl and Kurt Diemberger attempted Chogolisa in 1957 after they had successfully summitted Broad Peak behind Marcus Schmuck and Fritz Wintersteller a few weeks earlier.

Col.subject: World Geography
Col.question: What is Col? Lowest point on a mountain ridge between two peaks.
Col.fact: A col in geomorphology is the lowest point on a mountain ridge between two peaks.   Particularly rugged and forbidding cols in the terrain are usually called notches.

Dolomites.subject: World Geography
Dolomites.question: What is Dolomites? Mountain range in the Italian Alps.
Dolomites.fact: The Dolomites (Italian: Dolomiti, pronounced [doloˈmiːti]) or Pale Mountains (Italian: Monti Pallidi) are a mountain range in northeastern Italy.   The Dolomites are in the regions of Veneto, Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol and Friuli-Venezia Giulia, covering an area shared between the provinces of Belluno, Vicenza, Verona, Trentino, South Tyrol, Udine and Pordenone.

Dolomites.subject: World Geography
Dolomites.question: On 26 June _____, the Dolomites were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Dolomites.fact: On 26 June 2009, the Dolomites were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Ehrenbürg.subject: World Geography
Ehrenbürg.question: What is Ehrenbürg? Butte in Bavaria, Germany.
Ehrenbürg.fact: The Ehrenbürg (German pronunciation: [ˈeːʁənˌbʏʁk]) is a double-peaked butte on the edge of the Franconian Jura in Bavaria, Germany.

Double Peak (Washington).subject: World Geography
Double Peak (Washington).question: What is Double Peak (Washington)? Mountain in Washington (state), United States.
Double Peak (Washington).fact: Double Peak is a 6,199-foot (1,889 m) double summit mountain in Mount Rainier National Park in Pierce County of Washington state.   Part of the Cascade Range, it is situated northwest of Shriner Peak, south of Governors Ridge, and southeast of the Cowlitz Chimneys.

1938 USDA soil taxonomy.question: What is 1938 USDA soil taxonomy? Early classification system of soils in the US.

AASHTO Soil Classification System.question: What is AASHTO Soil Classification System? Classification of soils for road-construction purposes.
AASHTO Soil Classification System.fact: The AASHTO Soil Classification System was developed by the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials, and is used as a guide for the classification of soils and soil-aggregate mixtures for highway construction purposes.

AASHTO Soil Classification System.subject: World Geography

Acrisol.subject: World Geography
Acrisol.question: What is Acrisol? Soil type.
Acrisol.fact: An Acrisol is a Reference Soil Group of the World Reference Base for Soil Resources (WRB).   In the USDA soil taxonomy, Acrisols correspond to the Humult, Udult, and Ustult suborders of the Ultisols and also to Oxisols with a kandic horizon and to some Alfisols.

Acta Agriculturae Scandinavica B.question: What is Acta Agriculturae Scandinavica B? Academic journal.
Acta Agriculturae Scandinavica B.fact: Soil and Plant Science is a peer-reviewed scientific journal published by Taylor & Francis on behalf of the Nordic Association of Agricultural Scientists.   It covers environmental sciences, botany, earth sciences, physical geography, ecology, and the soil sciences of relevance to agriculture.
